<reason>Both sides were strong and motion-facing, and PRO deserves credit for taking the "even when" clause head-on, for the veto-legitimacy frame, and for the sharpest single pressure line (a consent unit defined as the release-zone majority returns "no" by construction; acceptance follows coexistence, so demanding prior consent locks the key inside the room). But CON did more damaging structural work. It correctly showed that PRO's central map (Germany, France, Alps, Scandinavia) is natural recolonisation rather than the deliberate release the motion actually describes, which hollowed out PRO's Rebuttal 1 centrepiece; it cleanly defused PRO's best turn by noting a consent rule does not withdraw fencing/compensation from wolves that walk in; and it distinguished the burden on sporting estates (a spreadsheet) from the burden on a shepherd, blunting PRO's "culling is imposed too" symmetry. CON also answered PRO's pressure questions directly and with structure (consenting unit, non-binding consent, and a concrete outcome-based culling reform with independent deer and sapling counts and government stalkers at the estate's cost), then converted that into an unanswered verification asymmetry: you cannot hide ten thousand red deer, but a buried lynx is invisible. Two specific CON hits went entirely unanswered — the lynx/red-deer ecological mismatch and the verified-culling counterfactual — and PRO's closing, its last chance, ignored both while CON's closing inverted PRO's own urgency framing ("a lynx shot in month three regenerates nothing"). PRO did land a genuine answer to CON's loaded "name one" question with Switzerland, Yellowstone and sea eagles, and CON's Switzerland rejoinder concedes establishment happened despite hostility, so this is close. But since CON conceded the ecology and disputed only necessity and durability, PRO needed the culling alternative to be dead, and it left CON's strongest version of that alternative standing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 1 point that every case on PRO's map was natural recolonisation, not deliberate release — plus the follow-up that a consent rule still funds coexistence with wolves that arrive on their own — simultaneously stripped PRO's evidence base and neutralised PRO's cleverest turn, and PRO never fully recovered the distinction between "crates and paws."</best_rebuttal>
